sections.title: What a wave is
equations: \text{waves transfer energy and information, not matter}

parts.title: The statement and the evidence
parts.html:
Waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter. Drop a stone in a pond and the ripples spread out, but the water does not flow outwards; shout across a room and the sound arrives, but no wind blows from your mouth.

Evidence with water waves: a cork or a duck on the water bobs up and down (oscillates) as the ripples pass, but it stays in the same place — it is not carried along. So the wave travels, the water does not.

Evidence with sound: a loudspeaker cone vibrates back and forth and the sound reaches you across the room, but the air does not rush from the speaker to you (a candle flame in front of it flickers but is not blown out; dust in front of a speaker vibrates in place). The air particles oscillate about fixed positions; the wave passes through them.

The energy is real: sea waves move boats and erode cliffs; sound waves make your eardrum move.

parts.title: Evidence question
parts.question: A student watches a leaf floating on a pond as ripples pass. Explain how the leaf's movement shows that the wave, and not the water, travels across the pond. (2 marks)
steps: Observation: the leaf moves up and down (oscillates) as each ripple passes…
Conclusion: …but it does not move along with the ripples — it stays in the same place. So the water only oscillates; it is the wave (the energy) that travels across the pond.

questions.text: State what a wave transfers, and what it does not transfer. (2)
questions.model:

  • …without transferring matter (the medium does not travel).

The wave travels but the water does not
The cork is too heavy to move
questions.explain: The water only oscillates; the wave (energy) travels.

questions.model:

  • The sound still arrives at the listener, so the wave has travelled through the air without the air moving across the room.

sections.blurb: A wave carries energy (and information) from one place to another without carrying the material along with it. The evidence is that the water or the air only oscillates; it does not travel.

sections.title: Amplitude, wavelength, frequency, period, wavefront

parts.title: The definitions
parts.html:
TermDefinitionUnit
Amplitudethe maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed (rest) positionm
Wavelength λthe distance from a point on one wave to the same point on the next wave (crest to crest, compression to compression)m
Frequency fthe number of waves passing a point per second (or produced per second)Hz (hertz, = per second)
Period Tthe time for one complete wave to pass a point (one full oscillation)s
Wave velocitythe speed (and direction) at which the wave (energy) travels — not the speed of the oscillating particlesm/s
Wavefronta line joining points that are at the same stage of the wave (e.g. all the crests) — the lines you see in a ripple tank; the wave travels at right angles to its wavefronts—

Traps: amplitude is not crest-to-trough (that is twice the amplitude). Frequency is not "how fast the wave goes" — that is wave speed. A louder sound has a bigger amplitude; a higher-pitched sound has a higher frequency. The 2022 report: "learn the difference between frequency and loudness of a sound."

parts.title: Reading the diagram
parts.question: On the diagram above, a crest is 6 cm above the undisturbed position and the crests are 24 cm apart. State the amplitude and the wavelength. (2 marks)
steps: Amplitude: rest position to crest = 6 cm (0.06 m). Not 12 cm, which is crest to trough.
Wavelength: crest to next crest = 24 cm (0.24 m).

questions.explain: Crest to trough is half a wavelength; crest to the next crest is 20 cm.

sections.title: Transverse and longitudinal waves

parts.title: The two kinds
parts.html:
Transverse: the oscillations (vibrations) are at right angles (perpendicular) to the direction of energy transfer. Examples: all electromagnetic waves (light, radio…), water surface waves (ripples), waves on a string, seismic S waves.

Longitudinal: the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer. The medium is squashed into compressions and stretched into rarefactions. Examples: sound (and ultrasound and infrasound), seismic P waves, a pushed slinky.

The mark-scheme phrase (June 2025 Q3(b)(ii)): "oscillations or vibrations perpendicular to the direction of travel of the wave" for transverse. Say oscillations, and say which direction they are compared with.

All mechanical waves — sound, water, seismic, waves on a string, whichever kind — need a medium to travel through; sound cannot cross a vacuum. Electromagnetic waves are the exception: they need no medium.

parts.title: Explaining the difference
parts.question: Explain the difference between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave, giving an example of each. (3 marks)
steps: Transverse: the oscillations are at right angles to the direction the wave travels — e.g. light / water surface waves.
Longitudinal: the oscillations are parallel to the direction the wave travels, producing compressions and rarefactions — e.g. sound.
Examples named correctly for both (third mark).

questions.text: Which of these is a longitudinal wave?
questions.explain: Sound is longitudinal; the others are transverse.

questions.text: Describe how the particles of air move as a sound wave passes. (2)
questions.model:
• They oscillate (vibrate) back and forth about a fixed position…
  • …parallel to the direction the sound travels, forming compressions and rarefactions.

questions.text: An earthquake produces P waves and S waves. State which is longitudinal and which is transverse. (2)
questions.model:
• P waves: longitudinal.
  • S waves: transverse.

questions.text: A rock is in the path of a seismic S wave. Describe how the rock moves. (2)
questions.model:
• It oscillates (vibrates)…
  • …perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction the wave travels (S waves are transverse).

questions.text: What is a compression in a sound wave?
options: A region where the air particles are closer together (higher pressure)
A region where the air particles are further apart
questions.explain: Compression = particles bunched; rarefaction = particles spread out.

questions.text: Explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum but light can. (2)
questions.model:
• Sound is a longitudinal wave that needs particles to oscillate (a medium to compress); a vacuum has none.
  • Light is an electromagnetic wave that does not need a medium.

checklist: Define transverse and longitudinal waves in terms of the direction of oscillation
Give the examples: sound (L), electromagnetic (T), water surface (T), seismic P (L) and S (T)
Use the words compression and rarefaction for a longitudinal wave
sections.blurb: Two kinds of wave, told apart by the direction of the oscillations compared with the direction the wave travels. Sound is longitudinal; light and all EM waves are transverse; water-surface waves are transverse; earthquakes send out both.

sections.title: The wave equations: v = fλ and v = x/t

parts.title: Two equations for all waves
parts.html:
$$v = f \times \lambda \qquad\qquad v = \dfrac{x}{t}$$

SymbolQuantityUnit
$v$wave speed (velocity)m/s
$f$frequencyHz
$\lambda$wavelengthm
$x$distance travelledm
$t$time takens

Why $v = f\lambda$ works: $f$ waves pass each second and each is $\lambda$ long, so the front of the wave moves $f \times \lambda$ metres every second.

Typical speeds: sound in air about 340 m/s (330 is also used), sound in water about 1500 m/s, light and all EM waves 3 × 10⁸ m/s, ripples in a tank a few tens of cm/s.

The June 2023 scheme (Q1(a)): $f = 330 \div 0.011 = 30\,000$ Hz; 30, 300 or 3000 (a power-of-ten slip from the 11 mm) got one mark of two. Convert first, substitute into the original equation, then rearrange — the 2022 report: "substitute in the original equation to be sure of getting a mark for this".

parts.title: Frequency from wavelength
parts.question: A bat's call travels at 330 m/s and has a wavelength of 11 mm. Calculate its frequency.
steps: Convert: $11\ \text{mm} = 0.011$ m.
Equation: $v = f \times \lambda \;\Rightarrow\; f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda}$
Working: $f = \dfrac{330}{0.011}$
Units: Hz

Ultrasound of frequency 1.5 MHz travels through water at 1500 m/s. Calculate its wavelength.
Thunder is heard 4.0 s after the lightning. Sound travels at 340 m/s. Calculate the distance to the storm.
Water waves in a tank have a frequency of 5 Hz and a wavelength of 4 cm. Calculate their speed.
A sound wave travels 1700 m across a lake in 5.0 s. Calculate its speed.

checklist: Select $v = f\lambda$ and $v = x/t$ and say what each symbol is, with units
Convert kHz, MHz, mm and cm before substituting
Rearrange both equations
sections.blurb: Two equations, both on the list, both for every kind of wave. The first links speed to how often and how long; the second is just speed = distance ÷ time.

sections.title: Period and frequency

parts.title: One over the other
parts.html:
$$T = \dfrac{1}{f} \qquad f = \dfrac{1}{T}$$

If 50 waves pass each second ($f = 50$ Hz), each one takes $1/50 = 0.02$ s: that is the period. If a pendulum takes 2 s per swing ($T = 2$ s), its frequency is $1/2 = 0.5$ Hz.

Counting method: $f = \dfrac{\text{number of waves}}{\text{time taken}}$ — count the ripples passing a point in 10 s (or the oscillations of a vibrating ruler) and divide. Counting for a longer time makes the frequency more accurate.

On a displacement–time graph the period is the time from one crest to the next; on a displacement–distance graph the same gap is the wavelength. Check which axis is which before you read anything off (T1).

parts.title: Period from frequency
parts.question: A loudspeaker vibrates at 250 Hz. Calculate the period of the sound wave.
steps: Equation: $T = \dfrac{1}{f}$
Working: $T = \dfrac{1}{250}$
Units: s (4 ms)

questions.text: A wave has a frequency of 250 Hz. Calculate its period.
A pendulum takes 0.8 s for one complete swing. Calculate its frequency.
A student counts 24 ripples passing a mark in 8.0 s. Calculate the frequency of the ripples.
The UK mains supply has a frequency of 50 Hz. Calculate its period in milliseconds.
A wave's period is doubled. What happens to its frequency?
questions.explain: $f = 1/T$: doubling T halves f.

checklist: Use $T = 1/f$ and $f = 1/T$
Find a frequency by counting waves in a measured time
Read the period from a displacement–time graph
sections.blurb: Period is the time for one wave; frequency is waves per second. Each is one divided by the other — a 50 Hz wave has a period of 0.02 s.

sections.title: Measuring the speed of sound and of ripples

parts.title: Sound in air
parts.html:
Method A — a long distance and a stopwatch. Two people stand a measured distance apart (100 m or more, by trundle wheel). One bangs cymbals (or fires a starting pistol); the other starts the stopwatch when they see the bang and stops it when they hear it. Speed = distance ÷ time. Light arrives almost instantly, so the time measured is the sound's travel time.

The problem is reaction time (about 0.2 s) compared with a travel time of about 0.3 s over 100 m. The June 2023 scheme (Q6(a)) had candidates work out that 0.23 s of reaction time was 63% of the 0.364 s travel time over 120 m, and the improvement asked for was increase the distance — a longer time makes the reaction time a smaller fraction. Repeating and averaging helps too.

Method B — two microphones. Connect two microphones, a measured distance apart, to a data logger or oscilloscope; make a sharp sound in line with them; the logger records the time between the sound reaching the first and the second microphone. Speed = separation ÷ time delay. No reaction time, so much more accurate.

Method C — echoes: stand a measured distance from a large wall and clap in time with the echoes; time 20 claps, divide for the time of one round trip, and speed = 2 × distance ÷ time.

parts.title: Ripples in a tank
parts.html:
A ripple tank: a shallow tray of water, a vibrating bar (dipper) driven by a motor or signal generator makes straight ripples, and a lamp above casts the wave pattern as light and dark lines on a screen or paper below (the crests focus the light into bright lines).

Way 1 — time a crest: mark two points a measured distance apart on the screen and time a crest travelling between them (or time it crossing the whole tank); $v = x/t$. Better: time it over a longer distance, or film it and use the frame rate.

Way 2 — f and λ: read the frequency off the signal generator (or count waves passing a point in 10 s and divide); measure the wavelength by photographing the pattern with a ruler beside it, or by measuring the distance across ten wavelengths and dividing by ten (one gap is too small to measure accurately); then $v = f \lambda$. A stroboscope flashing at the wave's frequency "freezes" the pattern so the wavelength can be measured.

June 2025 Q3(a)(iii) gave two marks for either way: "time a wave crest over a known distance, then speed = distance ÷ time" or "count the number of waves in a specified time (to calculate frequency) then use $v = f \times \lambda$".

parts.title: Speed of ripples
parts.question: In a ripple tank the dipper vibrates at 6 Hz. A student measures the distance across 10 wavelengths on the screen as 30 cm. Calculate the speed of the ripples.
steps: Wavelength: $\lambda = \dfrac{30}{10} = 3$ cm $= 0.03$ m (ten gaps measured, then divided — more accurate than one).
Equation: $v = f \times \lambda$
Working: $v = 6 \times 0.03$
Units: m/s

sections.title: Waves at a boundary: reflected, refracted, transmitted, absorbed

parts.title: The four effects
parts.html:
EffectWhat happensExample
Reflectionthe wave bounces back off the boundary (angle of incidence = angle of reflection)echoes; a mirror; sonar
Refractionthe wave crosses the boundary and changes direction because its speed changeslight into glass; ripples into shallow water; sound into warmer air
Transmissionthe wave passes through the materiallight through a window; radio through walls
Absorptionthe wave's energy is taken in by the material (usually warming it)microwaves by water in food; sound by curtains and carpet

Refraction direction: a wave that slows down on crossing a boundary bends towards the normal; one that speeds up bends away from it. Light slows in glass and water; sound speeds up in water; ripples slow in shallow water. The frequency never changes (T3).

It depends on wavelength: glass transmits visible light but absorbs most ultraviolet; carpet absorbs high-frequency sound better than low; a thick wall reflects or absorbs high frequencies but lets the bass through. June 2024 Q10(c): carpets and curtains absorb more of the sound, so less is reflected back into the room; wooden floors and painted walls reflect it — "echoes / bounces around" was accepted for reflection.

parts.title: Which effect?
parts.question: A room with wooden floors and bare walls sounds echoey; adding carpets and curtains makes it quieter. Explain why. (2 marks)
steps: Carpets and curtains: they absorb a larger fraction of the sound that hits them (soft, fibrous materials).
So: less sound is reflected back into the room; the bare wood and paint reflect most of it, which is what you hear as echoes.

questions.text: Sound travels from air into water, where it moves faster. Which way does it refract?
questions.explain: Speeding up → away from the normal (opposite to light into water).

questions.text: State the four things that can happen to a wave when it reaches the boundary between two materials. (2)
questions.model:
• Reflection and refraction…
  • …transmission and absorption.

questions.text: Explain why a wave changes direction when it is refracted. (1)
questions.model: • Its speed changes as it crosses the boundary (and it meets the boundary at an angle), so the wavefront turns.

questions.text: A studio wall is covered in foam. Explain why. (2)
questions.model:
• The foam absorbs sound (its energy is transferred to the foam's thermal store)…
  • …so less is reflected and there are fewer echoes in the recording.

questions.text: Which is an example of transmission?
options: A black surface warming in sunlight
A ripple bending in shallow water
questions.explain: Through = transmission; echo = reflection; warming = absorption; bending = refraction.

questions.text: Give one example of a material that transmits one wavelength of electromagnetic wave but absorbs another. (1)
questions.model: • Glass transmits visible light but absorbs most ultraviolet (or: the atmosphere transmits visible and radio but absorbs X-rays; water transmits light but absorbs microwaves).

checklist: Describe the four effects at an interface and give an example of each

sections.blurb: When a wave meets the boundary between two materials, four things can happen, usually more than one at once. Which dominates depends on the materials and on the wavelength.

sections.title: Sound, the ear, ultrasound and infrasound

parts.title: Numbers and the ear
parts.html:
Human hearing: about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz (20 kHz). Ultrasound is sound with a frequency above 20 000 Hz; infrasound is sound with a frequency below 20 Hz. Both are longitudinal, like all sound; we just cannot hear them.

Sound → vibrations in a solid: the compressions and rarefactions of a sound wave push and pull on a solid surface, making it vibrate at the same frequency. In the ear: the sound makes the eardrum vibrate; the eardrum passes the vibration to the small bones (ossicles), which pass it to the fluid in the cochlea, where hair cells turn it into nerve signals. A microphone's diaphragm works the same way; a loudspeaker does it in reverse.

Why only a limited range: a solid (the eardrum, a diaphragm) can only be made to vibrate efficiently over a limited range of frequencies — its size, mass and stiffness set what it responds to. Very low frequencies do not make the eardrum move enough to be detected; very high frequencies it cannot follow. So we hear nothing below 20 Hz or above 20 kHz (and the upper limit falls with age). June 2025 Q1(c): why infrasound is not heard — either "the frequency is too low" or "the eardrum (named part) does not vibrate / respond at that frequency" — scored; describing ultrasound by mistake did not.

parts.title: Uses of ultrasound and infrasound
parts.html:
UseHow it works
Sonar (ships, fishing boats)a pulse of ultrasound is sent down; it reflects off the sea bed (or a shoal); the time for the echo is measured; distance = speed × time ÷ 2 (T4)
Foetal (pre-natal) scanningultrasound pulses from a probe reflect at the boundaries between tissues (different densities); the times and strengths of the echoes build an image; no ionising radiation, so safe for the baby
Exploring the Earth's core (infrasound / seismic waves)earthquakes produce low-frequency P and S waves; detecting where each type arrives shows the core is partly liquid and the Earth's density changes with depth (T5)
Also: industrial cleaning, detecting cracks in metal (an echo returns early from the crack — 2022 Q10(b))

parts.title: Why we cannot hear infrasound
parts.question: Elephants communicate with infrasound. Explain why a person standing nearby cannot hear it. (2 marks)
steps: Frequency: infrasound has a frequency below 20 Hz, which is below the range the human ear detects (20 Hz – 20 kHz).
The ear: the eardrum does not vibrate enough at such a low frequency to pass the vibration on, so no signal reaches the brain.

questions.text: State what is meant by ultrasound, and give the range of frequencies humans can hear. (2)
questions.model:
• Sound with a frequency greater than 20 000 Hz.
  • Human hearing: about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.

questions.text: Describe how a sound wave in the air makes the eardrum vibrate. (2)
questions.model:
• The compressions and rarefactions of the sound wave reach the eardrum and push and pull on it (pressure changes)…
  • …so the eardrum vibrates at the same frequency as the sound; the vibration is passed on to the small bones and then the cochlea.

questions.text: Explain why the human ear can only detect a limited range of frequencies. (2)
questions.model:
• The eardrum (a solid) can only be made to vibrate efficiently over a limited range of frequencies — its size and stiffness set what it responds to.
  • At very low or very high frequencies it does not vibrate enough to pass on a signal, so those sounds are not detected.

questions.text: Which is a use of infrasound?
options: Studying the Earth's core with seismic waves
questions.explain: Seismic waves are low-frequency; the others use ultrasound.

questions.text: Explain why ultrasound rather than X-rays is used to scan an unborn baby. (2)
questions.model:
• Ultrasound is not ionising, so it does not damage the baby's cells; X-rays could cause mutations.
  • Ultrasound is reflected at the boundaries between different tissues, so the echoes can build an image of the soft tissue of the baby.

questions.text: A whistle produces a sound of 25 kHz. Why can a dog hear it but a person cannot?
options: It is too quiet for people
25 kHz is above the human hearing range (ultrasound) but within the dog's
questions.explain: 25 000 Hz > 20 000 Hz: ultrasound to us, audible to a dog.

sections.blurb: Sound is a vibration passed from the air to a solid — the eardrum — and the ear only works for a limited range of frequencies. Above that range is ultrasound; below it, infrasound.

sections.title: Key words: state what is meant by…

parts.title: The definitions
parts.html:
"State what is meant by" asks for the definition. Learn these as sentences.

TermWhat to write (mark-scheme form)Not this
AmplitudeThe maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed position.crest to trough
WavelengthThe distance from a point on one wave to the same point on the next wave (crest to crest)."the length of a wave"
FrequencyThe number of waves passing a point per second; unit hertz (Hz)."how fast the wave is"
PeriodThe time for one complete wave (one oscillation) to pass a point; unit s."how long the wave lasts"
Wave speed (velocity)The speed at which the wave (the energy) travels through the medium.the speed of the particles
WavefrontA line joining points on the wave that are at the same stage of oscillation (e.g. all crests)."the front of the wave"
Transverse waveOscillations perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (light, water surface, S waves)."a wave that goes up and down" with no direction compared
Longitudinal waveOscillations parallel to the direction of energy transfer, with compressions and rarefactions (sound, P waves)."a wave that goes along"
CompressionA region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are closer together (higher pressure)."the crest"
RarefactionA region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are further apart (lower pressure)."the trough"
ReflectionA wave bouncing back from a boundary."the wave stops"
RefractionA wave changing direction at a boundary because its speed changes."the wave bends" with no cause
TransmissionA wave passing through a material."sending a signal"
AbsorptionA wave's energy being taken in by a material (transferred to its thermal store)."the wave disappears"
UltrasoundSound with a frequency above 20 000 Hz (above the range of human hearing)."very loud sound"
InfrasoundSound with a frequency below 20 Hz."very quiet sound"
EchoA reflected sound wave heard after the original."a repeated sound"

sections.title: Explaining wave types and the evidence
equations: \text{say: oscillations, and which direction compared with travel}

parts.title: The phrases that score
parts.html:
Transverse: "the oscillations are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer". Longitudinal: "the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer, producing compressions and rarefactions".

"Up and down" only works if you also say the wave travels along — the comparison is the mark. The June 2025 scheme for rock in an S wave wanted "oscillations or vibrations perpendicular to the direction of travel of the wave".

Demonstrations: on a slinky, push the end back and forth along its length for a longitudinal wave (compressions travel along; each coil moves to and fro along the slinky); flick the end sideways for a transverse wave (the hump travels along; each coil moves across). A marked coil shows the medium oscillates about a fixed point and does not travel — the evidence for 4.2.

Sound is longitudinal because the loudspeaker cone moves forward and back, pushing the air into a compression and then leaving a rarefaction, and these travel outwards in the same direction as the cone's movement.

parts.title: Why sound is longitudinal
parts.question: Explain why sound is described as a longitudinal wave. (2 marks)
steps: What oscillates: the air particles oscillate back and forth about fixed positions, making compressions and rarefactions.
Direction: these oscillations are parallel to the direction in which the sound travels (the direction of energy transfer) — which is the definition of longitudinal.

sections.title: Refraction of waves: direction, speed, wavelength, frequency

parts.title: Wavefronts turning
parts.html:
Think in wavefronts (the lines of crests). When a wavefront meets a boundary at an angle, one end reaches the new medium before the other. If the wave is slower there, that end lags, the wavefront swings round, and the wave now travels closer to the normal. If the new medium is faster, the opposite: away from the normal. If the wavefront meets the boundary square on (along the normal) every part changes speed together and the direction does not change — only the speed and wavelength.

Frequency is fixed by the source: the number of wavefronts arriving at the boundary each second equals the number leaving. So with $v = f\lambda$, the wavelength changes in proportion to the speed: slower → shorter wavelength (the wavefronts bunch up), faster → longer.

ripples into shallow waterslowershortersametowards the normal
sound from air into waterfaster (≈1500 m/s from 340)longersameaway from the normal
light from air into glassslowershortersametowards the normal

June 2023 Q6(b) (3 marks): "refraction is caused by a change in speed"; "sound speeds up entering water"; "light slows down entering water". Mentioning only that the wavelength changes was worth one mark at most.

parts.title: Ripples into shallow water
parts.question: Water waves in a ripple tank pass from deep water into shallow water, where they travel more slowly. Explain what happens to their wavelength and frequency, and to their direction if they meet the boundary at an angle. (3 marks)
steps: Frequency: unchanged — it is set by the dipper; the same number of waves arrive at the boundary each second as leave it.
Wavelength: shorter — $v = f\lambda$ with $f$ constant and $v$ smaller, so the wavefronts bunch closer together.
Direction: the end of each wavefront that reaches the shallow water first slows first, so the wavefronts turn and the wave bends towards the normal.

questions.model: • The frequency is set by the source: waves arrive at the boundary and leave it at the same rate (they cannot pile up or vanish).

sections.title: Echoes and ultrasound: the distance is half

parts.title: Halve it, and watch the units
parts.html:
The pulse travels to the surface and back, so $v \times t$ is the round-trip distance. Either halve the time first or halve the distance at the end — the June 2023 scheme (Q1(b), 4 marks) credited both routes and gave 3 of 4 for 5.94 m (forgot to halve) and the June 2025 report notes a candidate who "rearranged correctly but did not double the distance in the diagram". Write the halving as its own line.

Units: echo times come in ms ($\times 10^{-3}$ s) and ultrasound times in μs ($\times 10^{-6}$ s). Speeds: sound in air 330–340 m/s, in water about 1500 m/s, in body tissue about 1500 m/s, in steel about 6000 m/s.

Embedded calculation practice (the Echoes and ultrasound type) sits below the worked example.

parts.title: The 6-mark sonar answer
parts.html:
June 2024 Q10(d) asked how ultrasound is used to measure the depth of the sea. Level 3 (5–6) needed, in a logical order: a pulse of ultrasound (above 20 kHz; "sonar" accepted) is emitted from a device on the boat; it travels through the water and is reflected by the sea bed; it returns to a detector on the boat; the time between emission and return is measured; the speed of sound in water is known; distance = speed × time; and the distance (or the time) is halved because the pulse went down and back. "Two or more of ultrasound, pulse, halving and the calculation step" separated Level 3 from Level 2.

Crack detection (2022 Q10(b)): a pulse into a metal bar reflects from the far end; if there is a crack, part of the pulse reflects from the crack earlier (shorter distance), and the pulse from the far end is smaller because some of the energy has already been reflected — the amplitude of a wave shows the energy it carries. Foetal scan: pulses reflect at the boundaries between tissues; the times give the depths and the echoes build an image; no ionising radiation.

parts.title: Bat and prey
parts.question: A bat's call travels at 330 m/s. It hears the echo from an insect 18 ms after calling. Calculate the distance from the bat to the insect.
steps: Convert: $t = 18\ \text{ms} = 0.018$ s.
Round trip: $x = v \times t = 330 \times 0.018 = 5.94$ m (there and back).
Halve: distance to the insect $= \dfrac{5.94}{2} = 2.97 \approx 3.0$ m.

sections.title: Seismic waves and what they tell us about the Earth

parts.title: P, S and the shadow zones
parts.html:
P waves (primary)S waves (secondary)
Typelongitudinaltransverse
Speedfaster — arrive firstslower — arrive second
Travel throughsolids and liquidssolids only (a liquid cannot be sheared sideways)
Detectedalmost everywhere, but with a shadow zone where they are refracted by the coreonly within about 103° of the earthquake — not on the far side of the Earth

Conclusions (what the examiners mark): S waves are not detected on the far side of the Earth → S waves cannot pass through the core → the outer core is liquid. P waves are refracted (their paths curve, and they bend sharply at the core boundary, leaving a P-wave shadow zone) → their speed changes with depth → the density of the Earth changes with depth, and the core is denser. Both wave types curve gradually through the mantle because the density, and so the speed, increases with depth.

The 2022 report on the 6-mark version: stating observations ("no S waves are detected on the other side") without conclusions "scores only Level 1"; Level 3 "combined both observations and conclusions" — "remember to draw conclusions from your analysis of information".

parts.question: Seismometers on the opposite side of the Earth from an earthquake detect P waves but no S waves. Explain what this shows about the Earth's core. (3 marks)

Physics: S waves are transverse and can only travel through solids; P waves are longitudinal and travel through solids and liquids.
Conclusion: the S waves must have been stopped by a liquid on the way — the outer core is liquid.

sections.title: Core practical: speed, frequency and wavelength in a fluid and a solid

parts.title: Fluid: the ripple tank
parts.html:
1. Set up the ripple tank with a dipper driven by a signal generator; a lamp above projects the pattern onto a screen below.
  2. Frequency: read it from the signal generator, or count the waves passing a point in 10 s and divide by 10.
  3. Wavelength: freeze the pattern with a stroboscope (or photograph it with a ruler in shot); measure across 10 wavelengths with a ruler and divide by 10.
  4. Speed: $v = f \lambda$. Check by timing a crest over a measured distance ($v = x/t$).

Suitability: the ruler on the screen is fine for a wavelength of a few cm but the image may be magnified — measure the tank itself, or calibrate the screen; a stopwatch is too slow for one wave, which is why you count ten or use the generator's frequency.

parts.title: Solid: waves on a string
parts.html:
1. Attach a string to a vibration generator driven by a signal generator; pass the string over a pulley with a mass hanging on the end to keep the tension constant.
  2. Adjust the frequency until a clear standing wave forms — a fixed pattern of loops.
  3. Wavelength: each loop is half a wavelength; measure the length of several loops with a metre rule and work out $\lambda$.
  4. Frequency: from the signal generator.
  5. Speed: $v = f \lambda$. Repeat at other frequencies; the speed should be the same (it depends on the tension and the string, not on $f$).

Suitability: the loops are static so a metre rule works; the string's vibration is far too fast to time directly, which is why $v = f\lambda$ is used instead of $x/t$.

parts.title: Speed on a string
parts.question: A string vibrates at 40 Hz and shows a standing wave of three loops over a length of 0.90 m. Calculate the speed of the waves on the string.
steps: Wavelength: three loops $= 1.5$ wavelengths, so $\lambda = \dfrac{0.90}{1.5} = 0.60$ m (one loop is half a wavelength).
Equation: $v = f \times \lambda$
Working: $v = 40 \times 0.60$
Answer: $= 24$
Units: m/s

parts.title: Speed of sound in air, in full
parts.question: Describe how a student could measure the speed of sound in air. (6 marks)
steps: Step 1 — variables. I will measure the distance the sound travels and the time it takes; the speed is calculated from them.
Step 2 — equation. $v = \dfrac{x}{t}$.
Step 3 — set-up. Two microphones a measured distance apart (e.g. 2.0 m with a tape measure), both connected to a data logger / oscilloscope, in a line with the sound source.
Step 4 — measure. Make a sharp sound (clap) in line with the microphones; the logger records the time delay between the sound reaching the first and the second microphone.
Step 5 — use the results. Speed = separation ÷ time delay. (Or: repeat for several separations and plot distance against time delay; the gradient is the speed.)
Step 6 — accuracy. Use the data logger rather than a stopwatch so there is no reaction time; use a large separation so the delay is long compared with the logger's resolution.
Step 7 — repeat. Repeat several times and calculate a mean time delay.

facts.q: What do waves transfer, and not transfer?
facts.a: Energy and information — without transferring matter.

facts.q: Evidence that it is the wave, not the water, that travels?
facts.a: A floating cork bobs up and down as ripples pass but stays in the same place.

facts.q: Evidence that it is the wave, not the air, that travels (sound)?
facts.a: Dust or a candle flame in front of a speaker vibrates in place; the air does not rush across the room, but the sound arrives.

facts.q: Amplitude?
facts.a: Maximum displacement from the undisturbed position (rest to crest, not crest to trough).

facts.q: Wavelength?
facts.a: Distance from a point on one wave to the same point on the next (crest to crest). Unit m.

facts.q: Frequency?
facts.a: Number of waves passing a point per second. Unit Hz.

facts.q: Period?
facts.a: Time for one complete wave to pass a point. Unit s.

facts.q: Wavefront?
facts.a: A line joining points at the same stage of the wave (all the crests); the wave travels at right angles to it.

facts.q: Loudness and pitch of a sound depend on…
facts.a: Loudness: amplitude. Pitch: frequency.

facts.q: Transverse wave?
facts.a: Oscillations perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer: light and all EM waves, water surface waves, S waves.

facts.q: Longitudinal wave?
facts.a: Oscillations parallel to the direction of energy transfer, with compressions and rarefactions: sound, P waves.

facts.q: Which waves need a medium?
facts.a: All mechanical waves (sound, water, seismic, string) need particles; electromagnetic waves do not and cross a vacuum.

facts.q: The two wave equations?
facts.a: $v = f \times \lambda$ and $v = x \div t$, for every kind of wave.

facts.q: Speed of sound in air, in water; speed of light?
facts.a: About 340 m/s (330 also used); about 1500 m/s; 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

facts.q: Why does $v = f\lambda$ work?
facts.a: f waves pass each second, each λ long, so the wave advances $f \times \lambda$ metres per second.

facts.q: 11 mm, 1.5 MHz, 20 kHz in base units?
T and f?
Frequency by counting?
facts.a: f = number of waves ÷ time taken. Count for longer for more accuracy.

facts.q: Speed of sound with a stopwatch: the method?
facts.a: Large measured distance; see the bang, start; hear it, stop; speed = distance ÷ time; repeat and average.

facts.q: Why stand further apart in the stopwatch method?
facts.a: The travel time is longer, so the reaction time is a smaller fraction of it.

facts.q: Speed of sound with two microphones?
facts.a: Measured separation; data logger records the delay between the sound reaching each; v = separation ÷ delay. No reaction time.

facts.q: Speed of ripples, two ways?
facts.a: Time a crest over a measured distance ($v = x/t$); or frequency from the generator and wavelength from 10 wavelengths ÷ 10, then $v = f\lambda$.

facts.q: Four things that can happen at a boundary?
facts.a: Reflection, refraction, transmission, absorption.

facts.q: Which way does a wave refract when it slows down?
facts.a: Towards the normal. Speeding up: away from the normal.

facts.q: Why do carpets make a room less echoey?
facts.a: They absorb more of the sound, so less is reflected back into the room.

facts.q: Range of human hearing? Ultrasound? Infrasound?
facts.a: 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz. Above 20 000 Hz. Below 20 Hz.

facts.q: How does the ear detect sound?
facts.a: Sound makes the eardrum vibrate at the same frequency; the vibration passes through the small bones to the cochlea, which sends nerve signals.

facts.q: Why does the ear detect only a limited range of frequencies?
facts.a: The eardrum (a solid) only vibrates efficiently over a limited range of frequencies — too low or too high and it does not respond enough.

facts.q: Uses of ultrasound on the spec?
facts.a: Sonar (depth), foetal scanning (echoes from tissue boundaries). Infrasound/seismic waves: exploring the Earth's core.

facts.q: Displacement–distance vs displacement–time graph?
facts.a: Distance axis: the gap between crests is the wavelength. Time axis: the gap is the period ($f = 1/T$).

facts.q: Crest-to-trough on a graph is…
facts.a: Twice the amplitude (vertically) or half a wavelength (horizontally). Not the amplitude; not the wavelength.

facts.q: The phrase for transverse?
facts.a: "Oscillations perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer." Say oscillations, and say what they are compared with.

facts.q: On refraction, what happens to f, v and λ?
facts.a: Frequency unchanged (set by the source); speed changes; wavelength changes in proportion to the speed.

facts.q: Ripples into shallow water?
facts.a: Slower, shorter wavelength, same frequency, bend towards the normal.

facts.q: Sound into water?
facts.a: Faster (≈1500 m/s), longer wavelength, same frequency, bends away from the normal.

facts.q: Echo distance?
facts.a: Distance to the surface = $v \times t \div 2$ — the pulse goes there and back. Halve it, as its own line.

facts.q: ms and μs?
facts.a: × 10⁻³ s and × 10⁻⁶ s.

facts.q: Sonar in six points?
facts.a: Ultrasound pulse emitted; travels through water; reflected by the sea bed; time to return measured; speed in water known; distance = $v \times t$, halved.

facts.q: Crack in a bar: why is the echo earlier and the far-end echo smaller?
facts.a: Part of the pulse reflects at the crack (closer, so sooner); less energy reaches the far end, so its echo has a smaller amplitude.

facts.q: P waves vs S waves?
facts.a: P: longitudinal, faster, through solids and liquids. S: transverse, slower, solids only.

facts.q: What do the S-wave shadow and the P-wave shadow show?
facts.a: No S waves on the far side → the outer core is liquid. P waves refracted sharply at the core → a sudden change in density; curved paths → density changes with depth.

facts.q: Observation vs conclusion in the seismic 6-marker?
facts.a: Observations alone are Level 1; the marks are for the conclusions drawn from them.

facts.q: Core practical: fluid?
facts.a: Ripple tank: f from the generator or counting; λ from 10 wavelengths ÷ 10 (stroboscope to freeze); $v = f\lambda$ or time a crest.

facts.q: Core practical: solid?
facts.a: String with a vibration generator and a hanging mass; standing wave; each loop = ½λ; f from the generator; $v = f\lambda$.

facts.q: Why measure 10 wavelengths?
facts.a: The ruler's uncertainty is the same, so it is a smaller fraction of a longer length; dividing by 10 divides the error by 10.

facts.q: State what is meant by: amplitude.
facts.a: The maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed position.

facts.q: State what is meant by: wavelength.
facts.a: The distance from a point on one wave to the same point on the next wave (crest to crest).

facts.q: State what is meant by: frequency.
facts.a: The number of waves passing a point per second; unit hertz (Hz).

facts.q: State what is meant by: period.
facts.a: The time for one complete wave (one oscillation) to pass a point; unit s.

facts.q: State what is meant by: wave speed (velocity).
facts.a: The speed at which the wave (the energy) travels through the medium.

facts.q: State what is meant by: wavefront.
facts.a: A line joining points on the wave that are at the same stage of oscillation (e.g. all crests).

facts.q: State what is meant by: transverse wave.
facts.a: Oscillations perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (light, water surface, S waves).

facts.q: State what is meant by: longitudinal wave.
facts.a: Oscillations parallel to the direction of energy transfer, with compressions and rarefactions (sound, P waves).

facts.q: State what is meant by: compression.
facts.a: A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are closer together (higher pressure).

facts.q: State what is meant by: rarefaction.
facts.a: A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are further apart (lower pressure).

facts.q: State what is meant by: reflection.
facts.a: A wave bouncing back from a boundary.

facts.q: State what is meant by: refraction.
facts.a: A wave changing direction at a boundary because its speed changes.

facts.q: State what is meant by: transmission.
facts.a: A wave passing through a material.

facts.q: State what is meant by: absorption.
facts.a: A wave's energy being taken in by a material (transferred to its thermal store).

facts.q: State what is meant by: ultrasound.
facts.a: Sound with a frequency above 20 000 Hz (above the range of human hearing).

facts.q: State what is meant by: infrasound.
facts.a: Sound with a frequency below 20 Hz.

facts.q: State what is meant by: echo.
facts.a: A reflected sound wave heard after the original.

types.name: Wave speed from frequency and wavelength
types.method: Use this when you know any two of wave speed, frequency and wavelength. Wave speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength: put the frequency in hertz and the wavelength in metres, and the speed comes out in m/s. If the speed is given, rearrange to f = v / λ or λ = v / f.
commonErrors: Leaving the frequency in kHz or MHz instead of converting to Hz
Leaving the wavelength in cm or mm instead of converting to metres
Multiplying v by f when the question asks for a wavelength, instead of dividing
Forgetting that radio waves and light travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s

worked.question: A loudspeaker produces a sound wave of frequency 250 Hz. The wavelength of the sound in the air is 1.36 m. Calculate the speed of the sound.
steps: Known: f = 250 Hz, λ = 1.36 m. Unknown: v.
v = f × λ

practice.question: In a ripple tank the dipper vibrates at 4 Hz and the waves it makes have a wavelength of 0.05 m. Calculate the speed of the water waves.
practice.hint: Wave speed = frequency × wavelength; both values are already in Hz and m.
walkthrough: f = 4 Hz, λ = 0.05 m, find v.

practice.question: Waves on the sea pass a buoy with a frequency of 0.2 Hz. The distance from one crest to the next is 40 m. Calculate the speed of the waves.
practice.hint: The crest-to-crest distance is the wavelength; multiply it by the frequency.
walkthrough: f = 0.2 Hz, λ = 40 m, find v.

practice.question: A radio station broadcasts at a frequency of 150 kHz. Radio waves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the wavelength of the radio waves.
practice.hint: Change 150 kHz into Hz (× 1000), then rearrange v = f × λ to λ = v / f.
walkthrough: f = 150 kHz = 150 000 Hz, v = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, find λ.
v = f × λ → λ = v / f

practice.question: An ultrasound scanner sends waves of frequency 2 MHz into body tissue. In the tissue the waves have a wavelength of 0.77 mm. Calculate the speed of the ultrasound in the tissue.
practice.hint: Convert 2 MHz to 2 000 000 Hz and 0.77 mm to 0.00077 m before you multiply.

practice.question: A student counts 30 waves passing a point in a ripple tank in 10 s. The wavelength of the waves is 2.5 cm. Calculate the wave speed in m/s.
practice.hint: Find the frequency first (number of waves ÷ time), and change 2.5 cm into metres.

practice.question: A microphone connected to an oscilloscope shows that a sound wave has a period of 2 ms. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. Calculate the wavelength of the sound.
practice.hint: Frequency = 1 / period with the period in seconds; then λ = v / f.
walkthrough: v = f × λ → λ = v / f

types.name: Wave speed from distance and time
types.method: Use this when a wave front or a pulse travels a measured distance in a measured time. Wave speed = distance travelled / time taken, the same speed equation as for a moving object. Change km to m and minutes to seconds first; rearrange to x = v × t for a distance or t = x / v for a time.
commonErrors: Dividing the time by the distance
Leaving a distance in km or cm when the speed is wanted in m/s
Using the crest-to-crest distance (the wavelength) as the distance travelled

worked.question: A water wave travels 12 m along a swimming pool in 8 s. Calculate the speed of the wave.
steps: Known: x = 12 m, t = 8 s. Unknown: v.
v = x / t

practice.question: The sound of a starting pistol travels 1700 m across a lake in 5 s. Calculate the speed of the sound.
practice.hint: Speed = distance ÷ time; both values are already in m and s.
walkthrough: x = 1700 m, t = 5 s, find v.

practice.question: In a ripple tank a wave front travels 0.9 m across the tank in 6 s. Calculate the speed of the wave front.
practice.hint: Speed = distance ÷ time; expect a small answer because water waves in a tank are slow.
walkthrough: x = 0.9 m, t = 6 s, find v.

practice.question: A lightning flash is seen and the thunder is heard 4 s later. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. Calculate how far away the lightning was.
practice.hint: The light arrives almost instantly, so the 4 s is the time the sound takes: x = v × t.
walkthrough: v = 340 m/s, t = 4 s, find x.
v = x / t → x = v × t

practice.question: A P-wave from an earthquake travels through rock at 6000 m/s. Calculate the time it takes to reach a seismometer 1500 km away.
practice.hint: Change 1500 km into metres, then rearrange to t = x / v.
walkthrough: v = x / t → t = x / v

practice.question: A sound wave travels 1.7 km through air in 5 s. The frequency of the sound is 200 Hz. Calculate the wavelength of the sound.
practice.hint: Find the speed from distance ÷ time first (in m/s), then use λ = v / f.

practice.question: Waves travel 30 m across a harbour in 10 s. One wave crest reaches the harbour wall every 4 s. Calculate the wavelength of the waves.
practice.hint: Speed = 30 / 10; the time between crests is the period, so f = 1 / 4; then λ = v / f.

types.name: Period and frequency
equations: f = number of waves / time taken
types.method: Frequency is the number of complete waves each second, so count the waves and divide by the time in seconds to get a value in hertz. Period is the time for one complete wave, and it equals 1 divided by the frequency. Change milliseconds to seconds, and anything per minute to per second, before you take 1 over it.
commonErrors: Dividing the time by the number of waves when the question asks for frequency
Forgetting that 1 ms = 0.001 s before working out 1 / T
Treating beats per minute as a frequency in hertz without dividing by 60

worked.question: A student counts 20 complete waves passing a point in a ripple tank in 5 s. Calculate the period of the waves.
steps: Known: 20 waves in 5 s. Unknown: T.
f = number of waves / time = 20 / 5 = 4 Hz
T = 1 / f

practice.question: A vibrating ruler clamped to a bench completes 30 vibrations in 6 s. Calculate the frequency of the vibrations.
practice.hint: Frequency = number of vibrations ÷ time in seconds.

practice.question: The UK mains electricity supply has a frequency of 50 Hz. Calculate the period of the mains supply.
practice.hint: Period = 1 / frequency.

practice.question: An oscilloscope trace shows that a sound wave has a period of 4 ms. Calculate the frequency of the sound.
practice.hint: Change 4 ms into seconds first, then f = 1 / T.

practice.question: A dolphin produces clicks with a frequency of 20 kHz. Calculate the period of the sound. Give your answer in ms.
practice.hint: Change 20 kHz into Hz, find T = 1 / f in seconds, then multiply by 1000 to get ms.

practice.question: A pendulum completes 25 full swings in 20 s. Calculate the period of the pendulum.
practice.hint: Find the frequency from swings ÷ time first, then T = 1 / f.

practice.question: A resting heart beats 72 times in one minute. Calculate the period of the heartbeat.
practice.hint: Change one minute into seconds to find the frequency in Hz, then T = 1 / f.

types.name: Echoes and ultrasound
equations: distance to the surface = v × t / 2
types.method: Use this when a sound or ultrasound pulse goes out, reflects from a surface and comes back. The time given is for the there-and-back journey, so the distance to the surface is half of speed × time. The speed of sound (340 m/s in air, 1500 m/s in water, 1540 m/s in body tissue) is given in the question. To find a time, double the distance first and then divide by the speed.
commonErrors: Forgetting to halve: the pulse travels to the surface and back, so speed × time is twice the distance
Using the speed of sound in air for a pulse travelling through water or body tissue
Leaving a time in ms when the speed is in m/s

worked.question: A ship sends a sonar pulse towards the seabed and receives the echo 0.4 s later. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s. Calculate the depth of the sea below the ship.
steps: Known: v = 1500 m/s, t = 0.4 s for the round trip. Unknown: depth.
x = v × t = 1500 × 0.4 = 600 m (there and back)
depth = 600 / 2
depth = 300 m

practice.question: A hiker shouts towards a cliff and hears the echo 2 s later. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. Calculate the distance from the hiker to the cliff.
practice.hint: The sound goes to the cliff and back in 2 s, so halve the total distance.
walkthrough: v = 340 m/s, t = 2 s, find the distance to the cliff.
x = v × t = 340 × 2 = 680 m (there and back)

practice.question: A bat sends out a click and hears the echo from a moth 0.05 s later. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. Calculate the distance from the bat to the moth.
practice.hint: Speed × time gives the there-and-back distance; the moth is half of that away.
walkthrough: v = 340 m/s, t = 0.05 s, find the distance to the moth.
x = v × t = 340 × 0.05 = 17 m (there and back)

practice.question: An ultrasound scanner sends a pulse into a patient. The echo from the far side of the liver returns 0.2 ms after the pulse is sent. The speed of ultrasound in body tissue is 1540 m/s. Calculate the depth of the far side of the liver below the skin. Give your answer in cm.
practice.hint: Change 0.2 ms to seconds, work out speed × time, halve it, then change metres to cm.
walkthrough: x = v × t = 1540 × 0.0002 = 0.308 m (there and back)

practice.question: A fishing boat is in water 450 m deep. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s. Calculate the time for a sonar pulse to travel from the boat to the seabed and back.
practice.hint: Double the depth to get the distance travelled, then t = x / v.
walkthrough: distance there and back = 2 × 450 = 900 m, v = 1500 m/s, find t.
x = v × t → t = x / v

practice.question: In an ultrasound scan of a foetus, one echo returns from the near side of the head 0.08 ms after the pulse is sent, and another returns from the far side of the head 0.20 ms after the pulse is sent. The speed of ultrasound in body tissue is 1540 m/s. Calculate the width of the head. Give your answer in cm.
practice.hint: Find the depth of each side (speed × time ÷ 2, with times in seconds), then subtract.

practice.question: A survey ship's sonar echo from the seabed takes 1.6 s to return. The ship moves to a second position where the echo takes 0.9 s. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s. Calculate how much shallower the water is at the second position.
practice.hint: Work out the depth at each position (speed × time ÷ 2), then find the difference.

types.name: Reading wave graphs
equations: wavelength = distance from one crest to the next
period = time from one crest to the next
types.method: Check the horizontal axis first: on a displacement–distance graph the gap from one crest to the next is the wavelength, and on a displacement–time graph that gap is the period. Amplitude is the height of a crest above the centre line, not crest to trough. Read the values where the crests sit on gridlines, then use f = 1 / T or v = f × λ if the question asks for a frequency or a speed.
commonErrors: Reading a wavelength off a displacement–time graph: the gap between crests on a time axis is the period
Taking crest-to-trough as the amplitude: amplitude is measured from the centre line
Measuring crest to the next trough (half a wavelength) instead of crest to crest
Leaving a wavelength in cm when calculating a wave speed in m/s

worked.question: The graph shows the displacement of the water surface along a line across a pond at one instant. Use the graph to find the wavelength of the wave.
steps: The horizontal axis is distance, so crest to crest is the wavelength.
First crest at 1 m, next crest at 5 m.
λ = 4 m

practice.question: The graph shows how the displacement of a loudspeaker cone changes with time. Use the graph to find the amplitude of the vibration.
practice.hint: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the centre line (zero), not from trough to crest.
walkthrough: The centre line is at 0 mm.
Each crest reaches 2 mm above the centre line.

practice.question: A long rope is shaken so that a wave travels along it. The graph shows the displacement of the rope against distance along it at one instant. Use the graph to find the wavelength of the wave.
practice.hint: Distance axis, so read the gap between two neighbouring crests.
walkthrough: Crests are at 2 m, 10 m and 18 m.

practice.question: A microphone is connected to an oscilloscope. The graph shows the trace for a sound wave. Use the graph to find the frequency of the sound.
practice.hint: Time axis, so crest to crest gives the period in ms; change it to seconds and use f = 1 / T.
walkthrough: Crests at 1 ms and 5 ms, so T = 5 − 1 = 4 ms

practice.question: A float bobs up and down on water waves. The graph shows the displacement of the float against time. Use the graph to find the frequency of the waves.
practice.hint: Read the period from one crest to the next on the time axis, then f = 1 / T.
walkthrough: Crests at 0 s, 0.4 s and 0.8 s, so T = 0.4 s

practice.question: The graph shows the displacement of the water surface along a ripple tank at one instant. The dipper making the waves vibrates at 2.5 Hz. Use the graph to find the speed of the waves in m/s.
practice.hint: Read the wavelength crest to crest in cm, change it to metres, then v = f × λ.
walkthrough: Crests at 5 cm and 25 cm, so λ = 25 − 5 = 20 cm

practice.question: The graph shows the displacement of air particles along a line in front of a loudspeaker at one instant. The loudspeaker produces a note of frequency 340 Hz. Use the graph to find the speed of sound in the air.
practice.hint: Distance axis, so crest to crest is the wavelength in m; then v = f × λ.
walkthrough: Crests at 0 m, 1 m, 2 m and 3 m, so λ = 1 m
